title: Python DSA: Interview Code Patterns
description: Code-focused decision scenarios with real Python implementations. Review code, spot bugs, choose optimal implementations, and learn interview-ready patterns.

concepts.name: Hash Tables & Dicts
concepts.description: Python dicts and sets for O(1) average lookup. defaultdict, Counter, and complement-search patterns.

concepts.name: Two Pointers
concepts.description: Using two indices to traverse arrays from both ends or at different speeds. Key for sorted array problems and partitioning.

concepts.name: Sliding Window
concepts.description: Fixed and variable-size window techniques for subarray/substring problems. Reduces O(n²) brute force to O(n).

concepts.name: Linked Lists
concepts.description: Singly and doubly linked lists. Two-pointer techniques, fast/slow pointers, in-place reversal.

concepts.name: Stacks & Queues
concepts.description: LIFO and FIFO structures. Monotonic stacks, expression evaluation, BFS queues, deque for O(1) both ends.

concepts.name: Trees & BSTs
concepts.description: Binary trees, BSTs, recursive traversals, DFS/BFS on trees, tree construction from traversals.

concepts.name: Graph Algorithms
concepts.description: BFS, DFS, topological sort, union-find, shortest path. Adjacency list representation.

concepts.name: Dynamic Programming
concepts.description: Memoization vs tabulation, state transitions, space optimization. Recognizing DP substructure.

concepts.name: Heaps & Priority Queues
concepts.description: heapq for min-heap, negation trick for max-heap. Top-K problems, merge K sorted, median finding.

concepts.name: Binary Search
concepts.description: Classic binary search and its variants: bisect_left, bisect_right, search on answer space.

concepts.name: Backtracking
concepts.description: Systematic exploration with pruning. Permutations, combinations, constraint satisfaction, N-queens pattern.

concepts.name: Prefix Sum & Cumulative
concepts.description: Prefix sums for O(1) range queries. Combined with hash maps for subarray sum problems.

constraints: Exactly one valid solution exists
Can't use the same element twice
Must return indices, not values
prompt.question: What is wrong with this implementation?

options.label: It works correctly
options.description: The two-pass approach is valid and handles all cases.

options.label: Returns same index twice
options.description: For [3,3] target=6, seen[3]=1 overwrites seen[3]=0. Second loop: i=0, complement=3, seen[3]=1, returns [0,1] — but for input [3,2,3], seen[3]=2 overwrites index 0, so i=0 finds complement at index 2. However, single-element case: [5,x] target=10 with i=0 would use seen[5]=0, returning [0,0].

options.label: Fails for duplicates & can return [i,i]
options.description: The two-pass version overwrites indices of duplicate values AND can return the same index for non-duplicate cases where num == complement.

options.label: Returns indices in wrong order
options.description: It returns [i, seen[complement]] which might not be in ascending order.

explanation.tradeoffs: The two-pass approach can be fixed by adding `and seen[complement] != i` to the check, but the one-pass solution is cleaner, faster (single iteration), and naturally avoids both issues.
explanation.keyTakeaway: One-pass hash map: check for complement BEFORE inserting current element. This naturally prevents using the same index twice and handles duplicates correctly because earlier occurrences are already in the map.
explanation.commonMistake: Writing a two-pass solution and not checking `seen[complement] != i`. The one-pass pattern is both simpler and more correct — always prefer it.

constraints: Must return unique triplets only (no duplicates)
Array can have up to 3000 elements
Elements range from -10^5 to 10^5
prompt.question: Which version should you use in an interview and why?

options.label: Version A — skip-duplicates
options.description: O(n²) time, O(1) extra space. Manual duplicate skipping with while loops after finding a match.

options.label: Version B — set dedup
options.description: O(n²) time, O(n) extra space for the set. Simpler code, set handles deduplication.

options.label: Both are equivalent
options.description: They produce the same output with the same complexity.

options.label: Neither — use hash map approach
options.description: Sort + two pointers is suboptimal; use a hash map for each pair instead.

explanation.reasoning:
Version A is the interview-standard solution. It achieves true O(n²) time with O(1) extra space (ignoring sort) by skipping duplicates in-place:

1. `if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue` — skips duplicate first elements
2. After finding a triplet, the inner while loops skip duplicate second/third elements
3. No extra data structure needed for deduplication

Version B works but uses O(n) extra space for the set and hashing tuples has overhead. Interviewers want to see the skip-duplicates technique — it demonstrates understanding of the sorted invariant.

```python
# Clean interview version:
def three_sum(nums):
    nums.sort()
    result = []
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]:  # skip dup first element
            continue
        if nums[i] > 0:  # optimization: no valid triplet possible
            break
        lo, hi = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while lo < hi:
            total = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi]
            if total < 0:
                lo += 1
            elif total > 0:
                hi -= 1
            else:
                result.append([nums[i], nums[lo], nums[hi]])
                while lo < hi and nums[lo] == nums[lo+1]:
                    lo += 1
                while lo < hi and nums[hi] == nums[hi-1]:
                    hi -= 1
                lo += 1
                hi -= 1
    return result
```
explanation.tradeoffs: Version B is easier to write under pressure but shows less algorithmic skill. The set approach also has worse constants due to tuple hashing. The `nums[i] > 0: break` optimization in Version A is a nice interview bonus — if the smallest number is positive, no triplet can sum to zero.
explanation.keyTakeaway: For k-sum problems on sorted arrays: fix one element, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates by checking adjacent elements. This pattern extends to 4Sum, kSum. Always sort first.
explanation.commonMistake: Forgetting the `lo += 1; hi -= 1` after the inner while loops that skip duplicates. The skip loops move to the last duplicate, then you need one more step to move past it.

prompt.context:
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters — find the length of the longest substring without duplicate characters. Compare these implementations:

**Version A (set + shrink):**
```python
def length_of_longest(s):
    seen = set()
    left = 0
    max_len = 0
    for right in range(len(s)):
        while s[right] in seen:
            seen.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        seen.add(s[right])
        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
    return max_len
```

**Version B (dict + jump):**
```python
def length_of_longest(s):
    last_seen = {}
    left = 0
    max_len = 0
    for right in range(len(s)):
        if s[right] in last_seen and last_seen[s[right]] >= left:
            left = last_seen[s[right]] + 1
        last_seen[s[right]] = right
        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
    return max_len
```
constraints: String length: 0 to 5 × 10^4
String contains English letters, digits, symbols, spaces
Need the length, not the substring itself
prompt.question: Which implementation is more interview-optimal?

options.label: Version A — easier to reason about
options.description: The set + shrink pattern is more intuitive and clearly correct.

options.label: Version B — true O(n) with jump
options.description: The dict + jump version never backtracks left pointer, giving better worst-case.

options.label: Both are O(n), pick either
options.description: Both are linear time, the difference is negligible.

options.label: Neither — use Counter
options.description: collections.Counter is cleaner for tracking character frequencies.

explanation.reasoning:
Version B is strictly better. Both are O(n) amortized, but Version A's inner while loop can process the same character multiple times (e.g., 'abcabc' — when hitting the second 'a', it removes 'a' one by one from the left). Version B jumps `left` directly to `last_seen[char] + 1`, making each step O(1) with no inner loop.

The key insight in Version B: `last_seen[s[right]] >= left` checks that the duplicate is actually within the current window. Without this check, a stale entry from before the window would incorrectly shrink it.

```python
# Interview-ready version with clear variable names:
def length_of_longest_substring(s: str) -> int:
    char_index = {}  # char -> most recent index
    left = 0
    max_len = 0
    for right, char in enumerate(s):
        if char in char_index and char_index[char] >= left:
            left = char_index[char] + 1  # jump past the duplicate
        char_index[char] = right
        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
    return max_len
```
explanation.tradeoffs: Version A is easier to write from scratch and harder to get wrong. Version B requires the `>= left` guard which is easy to forget. In an interview, if you're unsure, Version A is safer. But if you can nail Version B, it shows deeper understanding.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Sliding window with a dict storing last-seen indices lets you JUMP the left pointer instead of SHRINKING one step at a time. The `>= left` guard is critical — it ensures you only react to duplicates within the current window.
explanation.commonMistake: Forgetting the `last_seen[s[right]] >= left` check in Version B. Without it, the left pointer can jump backwards if a character was seen before the current window started, breaking the algorithm.

prompt.context:
Reverse a singly linked list. Which implementation is correct?

**Version A:**
```python
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        next_node = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = next_node
    return prev
```

**Version B:**
```python
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = curr.next
    return prev
```

**Version C (recursive):**
```python
def reverse_list(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_list(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head
```
constraints: Must reverse in-place (O(1) extra space for iterative)
List can be empty or have one node
Return the new head
prompt.question: Which version(s) are correct?

options.label: All three are correct
options.description: A, B, and C all correctly reverse the linked list.

options.label: A and C only
options.description: Version B has a bug — it loses the next pointer before advancing.

options.label: Only A is correct
options.description: B has a pointer bug and C has a base case issue.

options.label: A and B only
options.description: The recursive version has incorrect pointer manipulation.

explanation.reasoning:
**Version B has a critical bug.** After `curr.next = prev`, the original `curr.next` is lost. Then `curr = curr.next` follows the already-overwritten pointer (which now points to `prev`), creating an infinite loop or losing the rest of the list.

Version A fixes this by saving `next_node = curr.next` BEFORE overwriting `curr.next`.

Version C is correct recursive reversal. `head.next.next = head` makes the next node point back to current, and `head.next = None` removes the forward link.

```python
# Interview-ready iterative (memorize this):
def reverse_list(head: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next
    return prev

# Pythonic one-liner using tuple swap:
# curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next
# This works because Python evaluates the right side FIRST,
# then assigns left-to-right. So curr.next is read before overwrite.
```
explanation.tradeoffs: The iterative version is O(n) time, O(1) space. The recursive version is O(n) time, O(n) space (call stack). Interviewers generally prefer iterative, but knowing both shows depth. The Python tuple-swap trick is elegant but explain it if you use it.
explanation.keyTakeaway: When reversing pointers in a linked list, ALWAYS save the next pointer before overwriting. The three-variable dance is: save next, reverse link, advance prev, advance curr. Python tuple swap does this atomically.
explanation.commonMistake: Version B's bug: overwriting curr.next before saving the original next pointer. This is the #1 linked list bug in interviews. Always ask yourself: 'Am I reading a pointer I already overwrote?'

prompt.question: What's the assessment of these two solutions?

options.label: First is O(n) and correct; second is O(n²) but also correct
options.description: The stack solution is optimal. The replace solution works but has poor time complexity due to repeated string scans.

options.label: First has a bug with empty stack
options.description: When stack is empty and we see a closing bracket, the `if stack` check fails and returns False — which is actually correct behavior.

options.label: Second is cleaner and preferred
options.description: The replace approach is more Pythonic and equally efficient.

options.label: Both have edge case bugs
options.description: Neither handles all edge cases correctly.

explanation.tradeoffs: The replace approach is a clever one-liner for code golf but shows O(n²) thinking. The stack approach is O(n) time, O(n) space, and directly demonstrates understanding of LIFO matching. It's the expected interview answer.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Stack = the data structure for any matching/nesting problem (brackets, HTML tags, expression parsing). Map closing→opening for clean lookup. Check stack emptiness before peeking/popping.
explanation.commonMistake: Forgetting `not stack` check before `stack[-1]` — causes IndexError on empty stack when a closing bracket appears first, like ')('.

constraints: Array is sorted in ascending order
May contain duplicates
Return the leftmost valid insertion index
Equivalent to bisect_left behavior
prompt.question: Which implementations correctly find the leftmost insertion point?

options.label: All three are correct
options.description: All three implement bisect_left correctly using different loop invariants.

options.label: Only Version B
options.description: A and C have off-by-one errors for edge cases.

options.label: A and B only
options.description: C has a bug with the result variable initialization.

options.label: B and C only
options.description: A returns wrong value when target is not in the array.

explanation.reasoning:
All three are correct implementations of bisect_left, using different styles:

**Version A** (`lo <= hi`, exclusive shrink): The classic style. `lo` converges to the insertion point because we only set `lo = mid + 1` when `nums[mid] < target`.

**Version B** (`lo < hi`, half-open interval `[lo, hi)`): This is how Python's `bisect_left` actually works internally. `hi = mid` (not `mid - 1`) because `hi` is exclusive.

**Version C** (explicit result tracking): Stores the answer whenever `nums[mid] >= target` and keeps searching left for an earlier position.

```python
# Interview-ready: just use bisect
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

# bisect_left: first position where target can be inserted
# bisect_right: last position where target can be inserted

# Manual implementation (Version B style, matches bisect internals):
def bisect_left_manual(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums)  # half-open [lo, hi)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid  # NOT mid - 1 (half-open)
    return lo

# For finding first/last occurrence:
def first_occurrence(nums, target):
    idx = bisect_left(nums, target)
    return idx if idx < len(nums) and nums[idx] == target else -1

def last_occurrence(nums, target):
    idx = bisect_right(nums, target) - 1
    return idx if idx >= 0 and nums[idx] == target else -1
```
explanation.tradeoffs: Version B (half-open interval) is most consistent with Python conventions and bisect internals. Version A (closed interval) is most common in textbooks. Version C is most explicit about what's being tracked. Pick one style and be consistent.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Binary search has exactly two decisions to make: (1) loop condition (`<` vs `<=`), (2) how to shrink (`hi = mid` vs `hi = mid - 1`). These must be consistent: `lo < hi` pairs with `hi = mid`; `lo <= hi` pairs with `hi = mid - 1`. Mixing them causes infinite loops.
explanation.commonMistake: Mixing loop invariant styles: using `lo <= hi` with `hi = mid` causes infinite loops. Using `lo < hi` with `hi = mid - 1` can skip valid positions. Pick one convention and stick with it.

constraints: O(1) time for both get and put
Capacity is at least 1
No OrderedDict allowed in follow-up
prompt.question: What data structures do you need to implement LRU Cache from scratch?

options.label: Dict + Doubly Linked List
options.description: Hash map for O(1) key lookup, DLL for O(1) move/remove operations with head/tail sentinels.

options.label: Dict + Python list
options.description: Hash map for lookup, Python list for ordering. Move elements by removing and appending.

options.label: Dict + collections.deque
options.description: Hash map for lookup, deque for O(1) popleft/append.

options.label: Dict + min-heap with timestamps
options.description: Hash map for lookup, min-heap ordered by access time for eviction.

explanation.reasoning:
Only a doubly linked list gives O(1) removal of an arbitrary node (when you have a reference to it) AND O(1) insertion at the tail. The dict maps key → DLL node, giving O(1) lookup + O(1) reposition.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=0, val=0):
        self.key = key
        self.val = val
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.cache = {}  # key -> Node
        # Sentinel nodes avoid null checks
        self.head = Node()  # dummy head (LRU end)
        self.tail = Node()  # dummy tail (MRU end)
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _remove(self, node: Node):
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _add_to_tail(self, node: Node):
        node.prev = self.tail.prev
        node.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev.next = node
        self.tail.prev = node

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        node = self.cache[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._add_to_tail(node)
        return node.val

    def put(self, key: int, value: int):
        if key in self.cache:
            self._remove(self.cache[key])
        node = Node(key, value)
        self._add_to_tail(node)
        self.cache[key] = node
        if len(self.cache) > self.cap:
            lru = self.head.next
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.cache[lru.key]
```

Sentinel nodes (dummy head/tail) eliminate all null checks in _remove and _add_to_tail.
explanation.tradeoffs: Python list: list.remove() is O(n), so put becomes O(n). Deque: no O(1) removal of arbitrary elements (only ends). Heap: O(log n) for push/pop. Only the DLL gives O(1) for all operations. The node stores the key so we can delete from the dict during eviction.
explanation.keyTakeaway: LRU Cache = Dict + Doubly Linked List with sentinel nodes. Store the KEY in the DLL node so you can delete from the dict when evicting. Sentinel nodes eliminate edge cases. This is a top-10 interview design question.
explanation.commonMistake: Forgetting to store the key in the DLL node. Without it, when evicting the LRU node (head.next), you can't find and delete it from the dict. Also, forgetting to delete from cache dict when evicting causes memory leak.

prompt.context:
Binary tree level-order traversal — return values grouped by level. Compare:

**Version A (BFS with level size):**
```python
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    if not root:
        return []
    result = []
    queue = deque([root])
    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)
        level = []
        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)
        result.append(level)
    return result
```

**Version B (DFS with depth):**
```python
def level_order(root):
    result = []
    def dfs(node, depth):
        if not node:
            return
        if depth == len(result):
            result.append([])
        result[depth].append(node.val)
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)
    dfs(root, 0)
    return result
```
constraints: Return list of lists, each inner list is one level
Left to right ordering within each level
Tree can have 0 to 2000 nodes
prompt.question: Both produce correct output. Which should you use in an interview?

options.label: Version A (BFS) — canonical approach
options.description: BFS with level_size is the standard pattern for level-order. Shows understanding of BFS mechanics.

options.label: Version B (DFS) — more elegant
options.description: DFS with depth tracking is shorter and avoids importing deque.

options.label: Either is fine
options.description: Both are O(n) time and space. Use whichever you're more comfortable with.

options.label: Version A, then mention B as follow-up
options.description: Lead with BFS (expected answer), then show DFS variant to demonstrate depth of knowledge.

explanation.reasoning:
Start with BFS — it's the natural/expected approach for level-order and demonstrates the `level_size = len(queue)` pattern that's reusable across many problems (zigzag traversal, right side view, level averages). Then mention the DFS alternative to show versatility.

```python
# Interview-ready BFS template (reusable for many tree problems):
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    if not root:
        return []
    result = []
    queue = deque([root])
    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)  # KEY: snapshot current level size
        level = []
        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)
        result.append(level)
    return result

# Variations using same template:
# - Zigzag: alternate level.append vs level.appendleft (use deque for level)
# - Right side view: take level[-1] from each level
# - Level averages: sum(level) / len(level)
# - Max depth: count levels
```
explanation.tradeoffs: BFS uses O(w) space where w is max tree width (could be n/2 for complete tree). DFS uses O(h) stack space where h is height. For balanced trees, DFS uses less space O(log n) vs O(n/2). But BFS is the expected pattern and more naturally extends to related problems.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The `level_size = len(queue)` snapshot is THE BFS template for tree level processing. It separates levels without markers. Memorize this — it's used in level-order, zigzag, right-side view, and many more.
explanation.commonMistake: Processing BFS without the level_size snapshot — just popping one at a time doesn't let you know when one level ends and the next begins. The snapshot captures exactly how many nodes are at the current level.

constraints: num_courses: 1 to 2000
prerequisites[i] = [course, prereq] means prereq must come before course
Return any valid topological order, or [] if cycle exists
prompt.question: This is Kahn's algorithm (BFS topological sort). What determines if there's a cycle?

options.label: len(order) < num_courses after BFS
options.description: If not all nodes were processed, the remaining nodes are in a cycle — they never reached in-degree 0.

options.label: A node is visited twice in BFS
options.description: If we dequeue the same node twice, there's a cycle.

options.label: Any in_degree goes negative
options.description: Negative in-degree indicates a cycle in the graph.

options.label: Queue becomes empty prematurely
options.description: If the queue empties while there are still nodes to process.

explanation.reasoning:
In Kahn's algorithm, only nodes with in-degree 0 enter the queue. In a cycle (A→B→C→A), none of the cycle nodes ever reach in-degree 0, because each depends on another cycle member. So they're never dequeued and never added to `order`. After BFS, `len(order) < num_courses` means some nodes are stuck in a cycle.

```python
# Interview-ready with DFS cycle detection alternative:
def find_order_dfs(num_courses, prerequisites):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    for course, prereq in prerequisites:
        graph[prereq].append(course)
    
    # 0=unvisited, 1=in current path (gray), 2=done (black)
    state = [0] * num_courses
    order = []
    
    def dfs(node):
        if state[node] == 1:  # cycle: back edge
            return False
        if state[node] == 2:  # already processed
            return True
        state[node] = 1  # mark as in-progress
        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            if not dfs(neighbor):
                return False
        state[node] = 2  # mark as done
        order.append(node)  # post-order = reverse topo order
        return True
    
    for i in range(num_courses):
        if not dfs(i):
            return []
    return order[::-1]  # reverse post-order = topological order
```
explanation.tradeoffs: BFS (Kahn's) naturally produces topological order and detects cycles via the length check. DFS detects cycles via back edges (revisiting a gray node) and produces reverse topological order via post-order. Both are O(V + E). Kahn's is more intuitive; DFS is more flexible for other graph analyses.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Kahn's algorithm: start with in-degree 0 nodes, process them, reduce neighbors' in-degrees, add new zero-degree nodes. If you can't process all nodes, there's a cycle. The length check at the end is the cycle detection.
explanation.commonMistake: In the DFS version, using only visited/unvisited (2 states) instead of 3 states (unvisited/in-progress/done). With 2 states, you can't distinguish a back edge (cycle) from a cross edge (already-processed node in a different branch).

constraints: Coins: 1 to 12 different denominations
Amount: 0 to 10^4
Return -1 if amount can't be made
Each coin can be used unlimited times
prompt.question: For a coding interview, which approach should you present?

options.label: Top-down — easier to derive
options.description: Start with recursion, add memoization. Natural thought process that's easy to explain.

options.label: Bottom-up — more efficient
options.description: No recursion overhead, better cache locality, no stack overflow risk.

options.label: Bottom-up, but explain top-down thinking
options.description: Write bottom-up code but explain how you derived it from the recursive recurrence.

options.label: Greedy (largest coins first)
options.description: Always pick the largest coin that fits. Simpler and faster.

explanation.reasoning:
The best interview strategy: think top-down (recursive), code bottom-up (iterative).

1. **Explain the recurrence**: 'For each amount i, try every coin c. If c ≤ i, then dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i-c] + 1). Base case: dp[0] = 0.'
2. **Code bottom-up**: No recursion limit, no cache overhead, clear iteration.

```python
# Interview-ready:
def coin_change(coins: list[int], amount: int) -> int:
    dp = [float('inf')] * (amount + 1)
    dp[0] = 0  # base case: 0 coins needed for amount 0
    
    for i in range(1, amount + 1):
        for coin in coins:
            if coin <= i and dp[i - coin] + 1 < dp[i]:
                dp[i] = dp[i - coin] + 1
    
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != float('inf') else -1

# Time: O(amount * len(coins))
# Space: O(amount)
```

Greedy FAILS: coins=[1,3,4], amount=6. Greedy: 4+1+1=3 coins. Optimal: 3+3=2 coins.
explanation.tradeoffs: Top-down with @lru_cache is fine for interviews and handles sparse state spaces better (only computes reachable states). Bottom-up is better for dense state spaces like this problem where most states are reachable. For very large amounts, bottom-up avoids Python's default recursion limit (1000).
explanation.keyTakeaway: DP interview pattern: (1) Define state — dp[i] = min coins for amount i. (2) Define transition — dp[i] = min(dp[i-c] + 1) for each coin c. (3) Base case — dp[0] = 0. (4) Fill order — smallest to largest. Always verify greedy doesn't work before using DP.
explanation.commonMistake: Using greedy (always pick largest coin). This fails for many coin systems. Only coin systems where greedy works are 'canonical' (like US coins). For arbitrary coins, you need DP. Another mistake: initializing dp with 0s instead of infinity — leads to wrong minimums.

prompt.question: Why is the index `i` needed in the heap tuple?

options.label: Tiebreaker when values are equal
options.description: heapq compares tuples left to right. If two vals are equal, it compares the next element. ListNode isn't comparable, so (val, node) crashes. The index i provides a valid tiebreaker.

options.label: To track which list the node came from
options.description: The index identifies the source list for potential follow-up queries.

options.label: Performance optimization
options.description: The index allows O(1) access to list metadata.

options.label: It's not needed — just use (val, node)
options.description: Python can compare ListNode objects by default.

explanation.reasoning:
Python's heapq compares tuples element by element. If two nodes have the same value, it tries to compare the next tuple element. `ListNode` objects don't support `<` comparison, causing:
```
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'ListNode' and 'ListNode'
```

The index `i` (unique per list) serves as a tiebreaker that's always comparable:
- `(3, 0, node_a)` vs `(3, 2, node_b)` → compares `0 < 2`, no need to compare nodes.

```python
# Interview-ready merge K sorted lists:
import heapq

def merge_k_lists(lists: list[ListNode]) -> ListNode:
    heap = []
    for i, head in enumerate(lists):
        if head:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (head.val, i, head))
    
    dummy = curr = ListNode(0)
    while heap:
        val, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        curr.next = node
        curr = curr.next
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next

# Time: O(n log k) — each of n elements pushed/popped once, heap size is k
# Space: O(k) — heap holds at most k elements

# Alternative without sentinel:
# Add __lt__ to ListNode: def __lt__(self, other): return self.val < other.val
# Then heap can store (val, node) directly
```
explanation.tradeoffs: Alternative: add `__lt__` to ListNode so nodes are directly comparable. But in interviews, you usually can't modify the ListNode class. The (val, i, node) tuple pattern is the universal solution. You could also use `counter = itertools.count()` instead of the list index.
explanation.keyTakeaway: When putting custom objects in a Python heap, wrap them in tuples with a unique tiebreaker index: `(priority, tiebreaker, object)`. This avoids TypeError when priorities are equal. Common pattern for any priority queue with custom objects.
explanation.commonMistake: Using `(val, node)` and getting TypeError on equal values. The fix is the tiebreaker index. This comes up in any problem using heapq with custom objects (merge K lists, Dijkstra with custom nodes, etc.).

Count subarrays with sum equal to k. Array may contain negative numbers. Review this code:

```python
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = 0
    prefix = 0
    prefix_counts = {0: 1}
    for num in nums:
        prefix += num
        count += prefix_counts.get(prefix - k, 0)

```

A colleague suggests using sliding window instead:
```python
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = 0
    left = 0
    window_sum = 0
    for right in range(len(nums)):
        window_sum += nums[right]
        while window_sum > k and left <= right:
            window_sum -= nums[left]
            left += 1
        if window_sum == k:
            count += 1
    return count
```
constraints: Array contains positive AND negative integers
Length: 1 to 2 × 10^4
k can be any integer
Count ALL subarrays, not just one
prompt.question: Which implementation is correct for this problem?

options.label: Only the prefix sum version
options.description: The sliding window fails with negative numbers. Prefix sum + hash map handles all integers correctly.

options.label: Only the sliding window version
options.description: Sliding window is more space-efficient and handles the general case.

options.label: Both are correct
options.description: Both handle negative numbers and produce the same result.

options.label: Neither handles all cases
options.description: Both have edge cases with negative numbers.

explanation.reasoning:
**Sliding window FAILS with negative numbers.** The `while window_sum > k` assumption breaks because removing elements from the left might increase or decrease the sum unpredictably when negatives are present. Example: nums=[-1, 2, 3], k=4. The sliding window misses valid subarrays.

The prefix sum solution works because of this identity:
- If `prefix[j] - prefix[i] == k`, then subarray `nums[i+1..j]` sums to `k`
- For each `j`, count how many previous prefix sums equal `prefix[j] - k`
- The hash map tracks these frequencies in O(1)

```python
# Interview-ready with comments:
def subarray_sum(nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
    count = 0
    prefix = 0
    # {prefix_sum: frequency} — how many times we've seen this prefix sum
    prefix_counts = {0: 1}  # empty prefix (sum=0) seen once
    
    for num in nums:
        prefix += num
        # How many previous prefixes make a valid subarray ending here?
        count += prefix_counts.get(prefix - k, 0)
        # Record current prefix sum
        prefix_counts[prefix] = prefix_counts.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    
    return count

# Time: O(n), Space: O(n)
# Key insight: prefix[j] - prefix[i] == k  ⟺  prefix[i] == prefix[j] - k
```
explanation.tradeoffs: Sliding window works ONLY for positive-integer arrays (or when you can guarantee monotonic behavior). For the positive-only variant, sliding window uses O(1) space vs O(n) for prefix sum. Always check: does the array contain negatives? If yes, prefix sum + hash map is the only O(n) approach.
explanation.keyTakeaway: prefix_sum + hash_map is THE pattern for subarray sum problems with negatives. Sliding window only works with positives. The hash map stores {prefix_sum: count}, and the key lookup is `prefix - k`. Initialize with {0: 1} for subarrays starting at index 0.
explanation.commonMistake: Using sliding window when the array has negative numbers. The window can't reliably shrink because removing a negative element increases the sum. ALWAYS check sign constraints before choosing sliding window vs prefix sum.

prompt.context:
Generate all subsets (power set) of a list of unique integers. Two approaches:

**Backtracking:**
```python
def subsets(nums):
    result = []
    def backtrack(start, current):
        result.append(current[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            current.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(i + 1, current)
            current.pop()
    backtrack(0, [])
    return result
```

**Iterative (cascading):**
```python
def subsets(nums):
    result = [[]]
    for num in nums:
        result += [subset + [num] for subset in result]
    return result
```

Now the follow-up: what if nums can contain **duplicates** and you need unique subsets?
constraints: nums may contain duplicates in the follow-up
Each subset must be unique
Subsets can be in any order
prompt.question: How do you modify the backtracking approach to handle duplicates?

options.label: Sort + skip same-level duplicates
options.description: Sort nums first. In the loop, skip nums[i] if nums[i] == nums[i-1] and i > start.

options.label: Use a set of tuples to deduplicate
options.description: Generate all subsets, convert to tuples, put in a set, convert back.

options.label: Use a visited boolean array
options.description: Track which indices have been used to avoid picking the same element twice.

options.label: No change needed — backtracking handles it
options.description: The i+1 parameter already prevents duplicates.

explanation.reasoning:
Sort the array so duplicates are adjacent. Then at each recursion level, skip a number if it's the same as the previous number at that level (i > start ensures we only skip same-level duplicates, not the first occurrence).

```python
# Subsets with duplicates (interview-ready):
def subsets_with_dup(nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    nums.sort()  # CRITICAL: group duplicates together
    result = []
    
    def backtrack(start, current):
        result.append(current[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            # Skip duplicate at same recursion level
            if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
                continue
            current.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(i + 1, current)
            current.pop()
    
    backtrack(0, [])
    return result

# Same pattern works for:
# - Combination Sum II (skip dups)
# - Permutations II (sort + skip if nums[i]==nums[i-1] and not used[i-1])
# - Subsets II (this problem)
```

Why `i > start`? At each level of recursion, `start` is the first index we consider. If `i == start`, this is the first choice at this level — always include it. If `i > start` and the value equals the previous, we've already explored a branch with this value at this level.
explanation.tradeoffs: The set approach works but is O(2^n) extra space for deduplication and can't prune early. Sort + skip prunes the search tree itself, avoiding generating duplicates in the first place. This is significantly faster for large inputs with many duplicates.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Backtracking duplicate elimination pattern: SORT first, then `if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue`. This works for subsets, combinations, and with slight modification (using a `used[]` array) for permutations. It's the universal dedup trick for backtracking.
explanation.commonMistake: Using `i > 0` instead of `i > start`. `i > 0` would skip valid choices in deeper recursion levels. The condition must be `i > start` to only skip duplicates at the SAME recursion level (same decision point).

```python
def next_greater(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    result = [-1] * n
    stack = []  # stores indices

        while stack and nums[i] > nums[stack[-1]]:

```

- i=0: stack=[], push 0. stack=[0]
- i=1: nums[1]=1 < nums[0]=2, push 1. stack=[0,1]
- i=2: nums[2]=2 > nums[1]=1, pop 1, result[1]=2. nums[2]=2 = nums[0]=2, stop. push 2. stack=[0,2]
- i=3: nums[3]=4 > nums[2]=2, pop 2, result[2]=4. nums[3]=4 > nums[0]=2, pop 0, result[0]=4. push 3. stack=[3]
- i=4: nums[4]=3 < nums[3]=4, push 4. stack=[3,4]
- Result: [4,2,4,-1,-1] ✓

prompt.question: What type of stack is this, and what invariant does it maintain?

options.label: Monotonic decreasing stack
options.description: Stack maintains decreasing order (top is smallest). New elements pop anything smaller, becoming their 'next greater'.

options.label: Monotonic increasing stack
options.description: Stack maintains increasing order (top is largest). New elements pop anything larger.

options.label: Regular stack, no invariant
options.description: The stack has no ordering property; it just stores unresolved elements.

options.label: Min-stack tracking minimums
options.description: Stack tracks the minimum element at each level for efficient min queries.

explanation.reasoning:
This is a **monotonic decreasing stack** (bottom to top: largest to smallest). The invariant: at any point, elements in the stack from bottom to top are in decreasing order.

When a new element is larger than the stack top, it 'resolves' all smaller elements by being their next greater element. Elements stay on the stack until something bigger arrives.

```python
# Monotonic stack template — next greater element:
def next_greater(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    result = [-1] * n
    stack = []  # monotonic decreasing stack of indices
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and nums[i] > nums[stack[-1]]:
            result[stack.pop()] = nums[i]
        stack.append(i)
    return result

# Variations:
# Next SMALLER element: change > to <
# PREVIOUS greater: iterate right to left
# Circular array: iterate 0..2n-1, use i % n

# Daily Temperatures (same pattern):
def daily_temperatures(temperatures: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(temperatures)
    result = [0] * n
    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and temperatures[i] > temperatures[stack[-1]]:
            idx = stack.pop()
            result[idx] = i - idx  # days until warmer
        stack.append(i)
    return result
```

Amortized O(n): each element is pushed once and popped at most once → 2n operations total.
explanation.tradeoffs: Brute force is O(n²) — for each element, scan right to find the next greater. The monotonic stack does this in O(n) amortized by resolving multiple elements in batch when a large element arrives. It's the standard approach for 'next greater/smaller' family of problems.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Monotonic stack pattern: maintain a stack in sorted order. When a new element violates the ordering, pop elements and use the new element to 'resolve' them. Key variants: next greater (decreasing stack), next smaller (increasing stack), previous greater/smaller (reverse iteration).
explanation.commonMistake: Thinking the stack is O(n²) because of the while loop inside the for loop. It's O(n) amortized — each element enters and leaves the stack exactly once. Total operations across all iterations: 2n.
